summary: Describes the messages and procedures of the NACK-Oriented Reliable Multicast (NORM) protocol. It provides end-to-end reliable transport of data objects or streams over IP multicast, with receivers asking for repairs by sending negative acknowledgments. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: When a teacher reads to a whole class, students only raise a hand if they missed a part. NORM works like that, so the sender repeats only what some listeners say they missed.

questions: how does nack-oriented reliable multicast work
how does norm reliable multicast use nacks
how does norm congestion control work
subtitle: Reliable bulk data delivery to a multicast group, where receivers only speak up when something is missing.

tldr.problem: Sending data reliably to many receivers at once is hard: if every receiver acknowledged every packet, the sender would drown in feedback.
tldr.mechanism: NORM receivers send a negative acknowledgment (NACK) only for missing data, after a random backoff that lets one receiver's request suppress the others. The sender answers with repair packets, preferably forward error correction (FEC) parity symbols that can fix different losses at once.
tldr.outcome: It is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes the Experimental RFC 3940. It also specifies a TCP-friendly congestion control scheme, and the RFC says it is not meant to suit every multicast reliability need.

facts.label: Message types
facts.value: NORM_INFO, NORM_DATA, NORM_CMD, NORM_NACK, NORM_ACK, NORM_REPORT

facts.label: Group size
facts.value: On the order of tens of thousands of receivers

today: RFC 5740 is a Standards Track (Proposed Standard) specification published in November 2009. It obsoletes the Experimental RFC 3940, and the metadata lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What NORM Is For
sections.content:
The NACK-Oriented Reliable Multicast (NORM) protocol provides reliable transport of data from one or more senders to a group of receivers over an IP multicast network. Its main goal is efficient, scalable and robust transfer of bulk data, such as computer files.

Senders and receivers can join and leave a session at will, with little control traffic and no tight timing coordination. NORM is meant to adapt to changing network conditions with little or no pre-configuration, and the RFC says it tolerates inaccurate timing estimates and lossy networks, including mobile and wireless ones.

NORM carries three kinds of content, called NormObjects: NORM_OBJECT_DATA (static data in memory), NORM_OBJECT_FILE (a stored file) and NORM_OBJECT_STREAM (an ongoing stream of undefined length, comparable to the reliable stream TCP offers). A sender can also attach a small NORM_INFO message to an object, so receivers that join late can learn what it is.

The RFC states that, in typical Internet environments, NORM will readily scale to groups on the order of tens of thousands of receivers. The reason is that the main limit on scale is the volume of feedback the receivers generate, and NORM works hard to keep that low.
sections.plainLanguage: NORM lets one person share a big file with a huge crowd. Nobody has to say 'got it' over and over. People only shout when they missed something.

sections.title: Sessions, Nodes and Objects
sections.content:
A NormSession is made of participants called NormNodes that act as senders, receivers or both. Each node has a preselected 32-bit identifier, the NormNodeId, which must be unique within the session. Two values are reserved: 0x00000000 is invalid (NORM_NODE_NONE) and 0xffffffff is a wildcard (NORM_NODE_ANY).

Every object is cut into FEC coding blocks and symbols. A FEC encoding symbol corresponds to the payload of one NORM_DATA message, also called a segment. With systematic FEC codes, the first symbols of a block are the original data and the rest are parity symbols. By default, parity is sent only in answer to repair requests, though a sender may send some proactively to make delivery more robust.

Objects are named during transport by the sender's NormNodeId, its NormInstanceId and a temporary NormTransportId. These transport ids are valid only while the sender is sending and repairing that object, and they can wrap in long sessions. NORM does not provide globally unique identification of content, so the application has to manage that if it needs it.

The protocol builds on the Multicast NACK building block (RFC 5401) and the FEC building block (RFC 5052). For congestion control it specifies a baseline scheme called NORM-CC, based on TCP-Friendly Multicast Congestion Control (RFC 4654).
sections.plainLanguage: Everyone in the group gets a name tag number. The big file is cut into small pieces, each piece is numbered, and a few spare 'fix-it' pieces can patch holes later.

sections.title: Message Formats
sections.content:
Sender messages are NORM_DATA, NORM_INFO and NORM_CMD. Receivers send NORM_NACK and NORM_ACK. A sixth type, NORM_REPORT, is reserved for experimental use. The spec assumes UDP encapsulation, and messages are independent of network addresses, so they work over IPv4 and IPv6.

Every message starts with a common header: a 4-bit version (1 for this specification), a 4-bit type, an 8-bit hdr_len counting 32-bit words, a 16-bit sequence and a 32-bit source_id (the sender's NormNodeId). Senders use sequence so receivers can estimate packet loss for congestion control. It is explicitly not used for reliability, which relies on object and FEC payload identifiers instead.

A NORM_DATA header adds an instance_id, a quantized grtt (the sender's group round-trip time estimate), a 4-bit backoff factor, a 4-bit gsize (group size estimate), flags, a fec_id, an object_transport_id and a FEC payload id. Receivers that see a new instance_id from a known sender should drop their old state for it.

The sender commands (NORM_CMD) have sub-types: FLUSH, EOT, SQUELCH, CC, REPAIR_ADV, ACK_REQ and APPLICATION. Header extensions let the protocol grow: a het value from 0 to 127 means a variable-length extension, and 128 to 255 means a fixed one-word extension.
sections.plainLanguage: Every NORM message has a little label on the front saying what kind of message it is, who sent it and how many labels came before it. Different message kinds do different jobs, like 'here is data' or 'I am missing piece 7'.

sections.title: The NACK and Repair Cycle
sections.content:
In the RFC's synopsis, the sender transmits numbered objects as NORM_DATA messages. Receivers track the sender's current transmit position and only NACK for content that comes before it. They start a NACK only at FEC coding block boundaries, at object boundaries, on receiving NORM_CMD(FLUSH), or after an inactivity timeout.

Before sending, a receiver waits a random backoff chosen from a range scaled by K_sender times the sender's GRTT. K_sender must be greater than one. The RFC recommends 4 for Any-Source Multicast and 6 for Source-Specific Multicast. While waiting, the receiver collects the repair requests it hears from others. If those already cover its needs, its NACK is suppressed and never sent. This probabilistic suppression is how NORM keeps feedback low.

When a receiver does send a NACK, it asks for FEC parity symbols rather than specific lost packets, as many as its erasure count for that block. Different receivers with different losses therefore ask for the same kind of thing, and one parity packet from the sender can repair several of them.

The sender collects NACKs for a period of (K_sender + 1) * GRTT_sender, then logically rewinds to send repairs, earliest position first, and goes back to new data afterwards. It prefers unsent parity and only falls back to explicit retransmission when it runs out. If a NACK asks for data the sender no longer supports, it sends NORM_CMD(SQUELCH). At the end of its data, it sends NORM_CMD(FLUSH) messages, one per 2*GRTT_sender, to prompt any last NACKs.
sections.plainLanguage: If you miss a part, you wait a random moment before raising your hand. If someone else already asked for the same thing, you stay quiet. The teacher then repeats it once for everybody.

sections.title: Round-Trip Timing and Congestion Control
sections.content:
All NORM timers depend on the group round-trip time (GRTT), the greatest round-trip time among active receivers. The sender periodically sends NORM_CMD(CC) messages with a timestamp. Receivers echo an adjusted timestamp in their NORM_NACK or NORM_ACK feedback, which lets the sender compute each receiver's round-trip time. The sender smooths these into a conservative estimate and advertises it in the grtt field of every message it sends.

Congestion control in the baseline scheme (NORM-CC) is an adaptation of TFMCC (RFC 4654). It is required in the general Internet unless another IETF-sanctioned reliable multicast congestion control mechanism is used. Sender transmission is rate-based, not window-based. The receiver whose loss and round-trip estimates give the lowest calculated rate is the current limiting receiver (CLR), and the sender adjusts its rate to what that receiver can handle. The calculation follows a TCP throughput model so that NORM shares bandwidth fairly with TCP flows.

The RFC says NORM operation without congestion control should be considered only in closed networks. Congestion feedback in NORM_ACK messages uses the same kind of timer-based suppression as NACKs to avoid a feedback implosion.

An optional positive acknowledgment procedure also exists, for applications that need explicit confirmation from named receivers. The sender lists them in the NORM_CMD(FLUSH) message or in NORM_CMD(ACK_REQ).
sections.plainLanguage: The teacher measures how long it takes a question to travel to the farthest student and back, and uses that to decide how long to wait. The teacher also slows down if the room gets too noisy, so other conversations are not drowned out.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Beyond the usual risks of IP multicast, the RFC points out that malicious hosts could NACK excessively to stop the sender from making forward progress. Receiver join and service policies, which let a sender ignore or limit misbehaving receivers, can be applied if this is detected. Replayed NACKs can also force a sender to resend repair data even when messages are authenticated.

NORM is compatible with IPsec, and compliant implementations must be compatible with the baseline IPsec mode in Section 7.1. That mode is meant for one sender with Source-Specific Multicast and unicast feedback. It uses transport mode security associations and requires that members receiving the keys are trusted, so it protects against attacks from outside the group only. The EXT_AUTH header extension is reserved for other authentication mechanisms.

The RFC says congestion control actions must not be postponed by a slow authentication scheme. It recommends automated key management, and says application-level integrity checking of received data is highly recommended, because FEC repair alone does not guarantee integrity.
sections.plainLanguage: Someone could keep shouting 'I missed it!' to keep the teacher busy. The fix is to check who is allowed to talk and to ignore anyone who keeps causing trouble.

sections.title: Registries and Changes from RFC 3940
sections.content:
This document creates three IANA registries: NORM Header Extension Types, NORM Stream Control Codes and NORM_CMD message sub-types. New values are assigned on a Specification Required basis. The registered header extensions are EXT_AUTH (1), EXT_CC (3), EXT_FTI (64) and EXT_RATE (128), and the one stream control code is NORM_STREAM_END (0).

Compared with the Experimental RFC 3940, the changes include moving the stream message start flag into a payload_msg_start field, defining the IANA registries, removing the restriction of receiver feedback rate to the local sender rate, fixing errors in some message format descriptions, and adding the IPsec secure mode and the EXT_AUTH extension.

fields.desc: Per-sender counter used for loss estimation, not for reliability.

messages.label: NORM_NACK
messages.note: After a random backoff; sent only if no one else already asked.

messages.label: NORM_DATA (repair)
messages.note: Fresh FEC parity where possible, sent after aggregating NACKs.

messages.label: NORM_CMD(FLUSH)
messages.note: At the end of the data, prompting any last repair requests.
